abstract: Zipf's Law, that word rank times word frequency in most texts is roughly a constant, may be empirically verified by students using software provided by the authors. Such investigations help students value the connection between mathematics and other disciplines.

articleTitle: Crash Tests and the Head Injury Criterion
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: The Head Injury Criterion (HIC) model has been developed to measure quantitatively the head injury risk in crash situations. Using a computer algebra system (here MAPLE), students are able to analyse results reported from a real crash test carried out with Mercedes-Benz cars. The discussion of the model provides first an excellent motivation for the Riemann integral, serves secondly as a piece of real consumer enlightenment, and demonstrates thirdly that the need to (over)simplify reality may produce hardly meaningful results, despite considerable mathematical expenditure.

articleTitle: Making the Most of Resources for Mathematics Found on the Internet
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: There are many useful resources for mathematics that can be found on the Internet and many lists of useful sites. However, it is not always easy for teachers to use the resources either for themselves or with their pupils. This paper looks at a number of interesting sites and considers the different ways in which the information available can be used as a teaching resource. It also provides practical guidance on how teachers might take information in text, graphic and file format and use it either for themselves or with pupils.

articleTitle: Planetary Orbits: Change of Basis in R3
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: This paper illustrates the usefulness of the change-of-basis idea commonly taught in introductory linear algebra courses. Planetary orbits (or orbits of artificial satellites) can be simply described using a basis for R<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> chosen so that the orbit lies in a coordinate plane. It is also desirable to express the planet's position in terms of a different basis chosen to simplify the earth's position with respect to the sun. The change-of-basis idea allows one to convert readily from one coordinate system to the other.

publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: In many applications of linear algebra a key element is often the solution of the linear equations MX = B. When the matrix M is non-singular, this presents no problem with the help of general-purpose software such as computer algebra or a spreadsheet. However, when M is singular or non-square, finding a solution may demand a computer program or specialist software. A method for solving MX=0 in all cases is described in this note and illustrated by a model of traffic at a T-junction. The method employs only array commands widely available on spreadsheets. The worksheet from the spreadsheet Excel (Microsoft Corporation, 1992) in which the model is solved is reproduced. It is proposed that the method exposes the student to ideas and techniques which may be hidden by other software.

articleTitle: On Travelling Together and Sharing Expenses (Examples of Investigation of Situations)
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: This paper describes real-life investigations, encouraging both teachers and students to consider possible solutions which require a grasp of the whole situation. The examples used require questioning and analysis and an overview of several factors to determine the optimum solution in each case.

publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: This paper presents an example of a mechanical system involving a rotating frame of references in which physical intuition may not readily predict all the equilibrium points. As such, the example has been used by the author to make a useful teaching point and to help students develop their intuition about other similar problems.

articleTitle: Can Routine Problems be Transformed into Non-routine Problems?
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: What type of mathematical problems helps students learn and apply diverse strategies during their learning experiences? This is a fundamental question that needs to be addressed in terms of the qualities of the instructional problems that might offer potential not only for class discussion but also as a way to assess die students' understanding of mathematics. The idea of using problems that can be solved by different forms or methods of solution could be an important step in showing the students the advantages and disadvantages to thinking of those different approaches. This paper shows anticipated solutions of two problems that could be seen as routine problems initially; but the approaches utilized to solve them could be used as a platform for the students to launch questions and transform them into non-routine problems.

articleTitle: National Grid for Learning—Sideshow or Mainstream?
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: The computer is most definitely here. What could/should we be doing with it? In particular, what benefits might it offer to teachers of mathematics? Here we attempt to give a brief survey of what is on offer now, and the way things might be going.

articleTitle: Stella: Sophisticated Dynamics without Complex Mathematics
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: STELLA is a graphical modelling system that runs on a Macintosh computer. This paper provides an overview of the package and illustrates how it can be used for modelling a simple predator-prey system. The paper then describes how Stella can be used for solving differential equations, and in particular, how it can be used for solving the differential equations that model the flight of a tennis ball that is subject to the effects of spin and air resistance.

articleTitle: Teaching Influence on Life-long Perceptions of Mathematics
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: Many people, both pupils and adults, appear frightened of mathematics or maintain that they hate it. This paper is the result of research into peoples‘ perceptions of mathematics in order to identify how different attitudes might develop. The research focused on the emergence of negative perceptions and the implication of these for learning mathematics and using mathematics in later life. Many factors were found to influence the development of an individual’s perceptions of mathematics, but school experience was found to be crucial and this paper highlights the responsibility of all teachers to promote mathematics positively.

articleTitle: Combinations, Probabilities and Sample Size. Investigations into the Mann–Whitney U test
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: The Mann–Whitney U test is often used by students studying geography, sports science or psychology, yet it rarely appears in A-level mathematics syllabuses. This is a pity, because it provides considerable scope for thought and investigation by the student with a more mathematical background. As a non-parametric test, it is widely used to test whether two samples are “different” (for data that are unlikely to have come from a population that can be modelled by a normal distribution). This article shows how the test can be explained from “first principles”, using simple ideas of combinations and probabilities of equally likely outcomes. The mathematics student can understand the logic behind the test and can determine the minimum sample sizes required for a test of significance.

articleTitle: Waking up to Maths with “Snap, Prattle and Pop”
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: A “screensnap” is a calculator screen image which students are invited to recreate on their own calculator screens. It can be used as the starting point for the teaching strategy described here. Students tackle a calculator-based challenge (creating the “Snap”), about which they will inevitably be engaged in purposeful discussion (“Prattle”). The seeds are now sown for teacher and students to look beyond the particular screensnap and address mathematical questions of greater generality (the “Pop” stage).

articleTitle: Eulerian Trails and Circuits in the Analysis of Domino Layouts
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: In this paper graphs are used to model complete domino layouts. This was done firstly following the rules of the standard domino game and then extended to modelling layouts following the rules of the domino game of Sebastopol. The use of graphs in modelling the Chinese domino set is then considered for both the standard game and Sebastopol. The graphs developed in the above are then used to answer some construction problems related to the two games.

articleTitle: Teaching versus Lecturing Some thoughts on the teaching of mathematics at tertiary level
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: Some examples of alternative styles of transmitting mathematical knowledge at tertiary level are discussed with a view to promoting debate on the issue. We emphasise processes rather than skills, and consider problem solving and peer tutoring.

articleTitle: The Internet-What's Really in it for Teachers
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: Some of the fundamental questions about what the Internet has to offer to busy working teachers are discussed. Is the learning curve worth the effort? Is the technology truly accessible yet? How are teachers to be motivated into trying it out? What are the gains for teachers themselves as apart from the pupils?

articleTitle: A Critical Panoramic View of Basic Mathematical Concepts
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: There are important reasons to guard against commonly occurring mathematical errors such as those found in dealing with division by zero, concepts of infinity and divergent series, as well as some of the rules of convention. It is shown that these errant views are widely found among teachers, and among authors of applied mathematics texts, and unsurprisingly, among their students. Sadly, these persistent errors do not exist in isolation in a classroom or academic text. Important conclusions are inappropriately drawn after applying these errors leading to further erroneous conclusions. Classroom experimentation is suggested both to confirm the occurrence of these errors and to apply the appropriate teaching corrective.

abstract: This article is concerned with the mathematics that exists in popular culture. The probability inherent in a TV quiz show is explored. The article analyses how contestants can maximise their expected prize money by using simple probability theory.

articleTitle: The Significance of Ideas in Undergraduate Mathematics: A Case Study of the Views of Lecturers and Students
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: This study considers the extent to which students are acquiring an understanding of mathematics as a whole and of the relative significance of different parts of mathematics to that whole. Lecturers and undergraduates were asked to give five “big” ideas appropriate to the first two years of a mathematics degree, and to give reasons for their choices. The study indicates that, even after two years of undergraduate mathematics, many of the students involved had not developed such an understanding, and concludes that developing such understanding, while also maintaining high standards in students' content knowledge, will become an increasingly important challenge in the future.

abstract: We re-examine fitting a “best” straight line to a set of data points. We highlight that the least-squares line does not necessarily coincide with a line chosen to satisfy our geometric intuition. This is done by analysing the changes to the slope and intercept of the least squares line by the addition of a single extra data point.

publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: The black body function for radiative heat transfer can be used as a real application in a number of different topics in A-level and first-year undergraduate mathematical methods courses. This paper discusses examples using the black body function in the areas of functions of more than one variable, differentiation, solving nonlinear equations and integration by substitution.

articleTitle: Micromaths: Dilations, Splines and CAD—As Easy As ABC
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: The development of new technology tools to enhance mathematics provides a special impetus and opportunity for enduring curriculum reform in several areas. This force for change is controversial and it is clear that as the direction of courses shifts new problems are emerging which need to be addressed. Teachers and lecturers need to identify essential skills which are technology independent as well as determine the most effective use of this new technology in the classroom.

articleTitle: Are the Proposed Reforms of Numeracy Teaching Sufficient for Success?
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: This article comments on current official proposals for the improvement of the teaching of numeracy in English primary schools; it raises four main concerns, based on the authors' experience of reforming mathematics teaching in a group of primary schools in the London Borough of Barking and Dagenham. (a) More investment needs to be made in developing detailed teaching materials than envisaged in current official proposals, (b) Current official proposals are based on dividing each class into subgroups by pupils' abilities; Continental experience shows that higher average standards are to be attained by whole-class teaching, and that this approach particularly helps weaker (slow developing) pupils, (c) Training in whole-class teaching methods needs to be carried out in a more thorough-going way than officially envisaged, (d) The National Curriculum in mathematics needs to be narrowed, and taken at a much slower pace, if the foundations of mathematics are to be consolidated by a much greater proportion of the class.

publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: The superior performance of Continental schools in laying the foundations of mathematical competence is reviewed through the direct observations of English teachers and headteachers. As part of the Primary Mathematics Initiative in the London Borough of Barking and Dagenham, run in conjunction with researchers from the National Institute, over 50 teachers have visited schools in Switzerland and Germany for a week at a time in a programme which began in 1994. Their observations have contributed to experimental reforms in classes in the Borough which are now in their second phase. The reforms aim to combat under-achievement in mathematics through the introduction of successful Continental pedagogy in the teaching of number. The pedagogy and its introduction into the Borough‘s schools are discussed and some criticisms which have been levelled at the reforms are addressed.
